warmup.q: You ask for a web page that lives on a computer in another city. When your request leaves the laptop, the address on its outermost envelope names one machine: the one that should take it next. Whose machine is that?
options: The computer in the other city that holds the web page
The café's router, the first machine on the way
The machine that turned the page's name into a number
Nobody's: it's addressed to everyone, and the right machine picks it up
warmup.why: The outer address only works across one hop, from one machine to the next one it can reach directly. Your laptop can't reach the web server's computer directly, so it addresses the outer envelope to the café's router and puts the web server's address on an inner envelope, which stays the same the whole way. Every router on the path tears off the outer envelope and writes a new one for the next hop. In this lesson's capture, the outer address belongs to the lab's gateway, its first router. The last option is a real thing, called a broadcast, but it's for questions to every machine nearby, and the next lesson uses one. The first option is the trap for anyone who pictures one wire from end to end.

sections.h: From one cable to the internet: four problems, four kinds of address
sections.html:
A browser does many things at once, so let's use a program that does one. curl fetches a web page from the command line, the window where you type commands. Ask it for http://example.com/, a page kept for examples, and it writes these 74 bytes of text (here, one byte is one character):

GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
Accept: */*

This is HTTP, the language that browsers and web servers speak. (A web server is a program on another computer that hands out pages when asked.) The first line asks for the front page, /. The others name the site and the program asking, and accept any kind of answer.

curl's job is to get those bytes to a web server it knows only by name. Let's design that from nothing. Four problems turn up, one after another, and each needs a new kind of address.

Start with two computers joined by one cable. Each has a network card, the part that turns bytes into signals on the cable (or into radio waves, for Wi-Fi) and back. Your computer sends the 74 bytes, and the other card receives them. With only two of you, nobody needs an address.

Add a third computer to the cable, or a third laptop to the café's Wi-Fi, and that stops working. Every card now hears everything that's sent. So each card needs a name, and each chunk of data needs a label saying which card it's for. That name is a MAC address: six bytes given to each card, written like 22:d2:d5:a2:32:a3. A chunk of data with this label on it is called a frame. The cards that can hear each other directly make up one link, and moving frames across one link is the job of the link layer. Ethernet is the rulebook for wired links. Wi-Fi has its own, but to your programs it looks the same.

Now the web server isn't on your link at all. It sits in a building full of computers in another city, many links away. Its card can't hear yours, and nobody could keep a list of every card on the planet. So we need a second kind of address that works across links, the way a street address works across towns. That's an IP address (IP is short for Internet Protocol): four bytes, written like 104.20.23.154. Between links sit routers, machines with a card on two or more links. A router reads the IP address on whatever arrives, picks the next link that leads closer to it, and passes it on, like a sorting office for post. Your computer needs to know only one router, its default gateway, and hands it everything that isn't for its own link. This is the internet layer, and a chunk of data with IP addresses on it is called a packet.

Reaching the right computer still isn't enough. The server runs many programs, and bytes for the web server mustn't end up in some other program. So each program that talks over the network gets a number, a port, like a flat number in a block. Web servers use 80 for plain pages and 443 for HTTPS, the encrypted kind. This layer, the transport layer, has a second job. Packets get lost, arrive twice or arrive out of order, and IP fixes none of that. TCP (Transmission Control Protocol), the set of rules curl uses at this layer, numbers every byte, sends again what goes missing, and hands over the bytes in their original order. A set of rules like this, which both ends agree to follow, is called a protocol.

Last, people type names, not numbers. Something must turn example.com into 104.20.23.154 before anything else can happen. That's DNS, the internet's address book. It's itself another program on the network, so it sits at the top, in the application layer, next to HTTP.

So the software that moves your request has four layers. Each one answers one question, with its own kind of address:

Layer Question it answers Protocol here Addresses in this request
Application what to say, to which name HTTP, DNS example.com
Transport which program, in what order TCP port 57236 to port 80
Internet which computer, across links IP 172.20.0.2 to 104.20.23.154
Link which card on this link Ethernet b6:99:4a:b0:80:7f to 22:d2:d5:a2:32:a3

Keep this table in mind for the whole track: every later lesson zooms into one row of it. You'll also hear the rows called by numbers from an older model, OSI: L2 for the link, L3 for IP, L4 for TCP and L7 for the application. So an "L4" load balancer, a machine that spreads requests over several servers, passes TCP connections on without reading them. An "L7" one reads the HTTP request to choose a server.

Two entries surprise most people. The destination MAC isn't the server's. It belongs to the gateway, the next card on your own link, as in the warm-up. And curl never chose port 57236. The kernel, the core of the operating system that owns the network card, picked a free port for this one connection. The Try it shows all four pairs of addresses for a live connection. Then we'll see how the layers fit around one request.

try.title: Find all four addresses
steps: Start the lab box from the labs folder: docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box. The lab box is a small Linux computer that runs inside Docker on your laptop. (Linux is the operating system most servers run, and Docker is a program that runs small, separate computers like this one, called containers.) You get a command line inside it, with every tool this track uses.

Run the commands below one at a time. The comment on each line says which address it prints. The line with exec 3<>/dev/tcp/... is a trick of bash, the program that reads your commands: it opens a TCP connection to example.com and keeps it open, so that ss, Linux's tool for listing connections, has something to show.
Match each line of output to a row of the table: the name and its IP address, your IP address, your port and theirs, and the gateway's MAC.

On a Mac there is no ip or ss. In the Terminal app, ifconfig en0 shows your IP address and MAC, netstat -rn -f inet your gateway, arp -an the MACs your Mac has learned, and lsof -nP -iTCP your open connections.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: getent ahostsv4 example.com | head -1 # name -> IP, through the resolver ip -br -4 addr show eth0 # your IP and prefix ip -br link show eth0 # your MAC ip route show default # where packets for the internet go exec 3<>/dev/tcp/example.com/80 # open a TCP connection and keep it ss -tn dst :80 # both ends of it: IP and port ip neigh show # the gateway's MAC, learned just now exec 3>&- # close the connection

try.expect:
From one run:

172.66.147.243  STREAM example.com
eth0@if149       UP             172.20.0.2/16
eth0@if149       UP             92:7e:7a:47:49:1b <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP>
default via 172.20.0.1 dev eth0
State Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port    Peer Address:PortProcess
ESTAB 0      0         172.20.0.2:50324 172.66.147.243:80
172.20.0.1 dev eth0 lladdr 22:d2:d5:a2:32:a3 REACHABLE

example.com has more than one IP address, so yours may differ, and Docker gives the box a new made-up MAC every time it starts. (The /16 after the box's address says how big its network is; lesson 3 of this track explains it.) Now look for what's missing: example.com's MAC appears nowhere. The only other MAC the box knows is the gateway's, at 172.20.0.1, the first router on the way.

aside.title: Why two addresses? Couldn't the IP address do both jobs?
aside.html: The two answer different questions. A MAC address belongs to the card: the maker gives it one, or the computer makes one up when it joins a link. So a link can deliver frames to a card before the computer has an IP address at all. That matters, because a laptop that joins the café's Wi-Fi must first ask the network for an IP address. An IP address belongs to a place in the network, so your laptop gets a different one in every café, the way your street address changes when you move. Keeping the two apart also let IP run over any kind of link, wired, Wi-Fi or mobile, each with its own way of naming cards.

sections.h: Envelopes inside envelopes: how the layers wrap one request
sections.html:
The four layers don't send four separate messages. They nest, like envelopes. curl hands its 74 bytes to the kernel through a socket. A socket is the kernel's handle for one conversation over the network, and a program writes to it and reads from it much like a file. Then the bytes travel down the layers inside the kernel, and each layer puts its own header in front: a few bytes that hold that layer's addresses and some bookkeeping.

  • TCP adds 32 bytes: the two ports, the numbers it uses to keep the bytes in order, some flags (single bits that mark things such as "this starts a connection") and a few options. 74 bytes become 106.
  • IP adds 20 bytes: the two IP addresses, a protocol number, a counter called the TTL (time to live) and a checksum. Every router lowers the TTL by one, so a packet caught in a loop dies at zero. The checksum is a number worked out from the header's bytes, so the receiver can spot damage. 106 bytes become 126.
  • Ethernet adds 14 bytes: the two MAC addresses and a type field. 126 bytes become 140, and the network card sends those 140 bytes as one frame.

Think of posting a letter. You write the letter: that's the HTTP request. It goes in an envelope with a flat number on it, the port. That envelope goes inside a parcel with the street address, the IP address. Then a courier sticks a label on the outside that says only which depot to drive to next: the MAC address. Each layer treats whatever the layer above handed it as a sealed parcel and never looks inside. This wrapping is called encapsulation.

At the other end, the kernel unwraps in the opposite order. That's where one field in each header earns its place: it says what's inside. Ethernet's type field, the EtherType, is 0x0800 here, a number in hexadecimal (base 16, marked by the 0x). It means an IPv4 packet follows, IPv4 being the version of IP with 4-byte addresses. IP's protocol field is 6, which means a TCP segment follows. A 17 would mean UDP, a simpler protocol that doesn't resend or reorder. And TCP's destination port, 80, picks the program. The kernel follows those three fields, one per layer, and hands the web server exactly the 74 bytes curl wrote.

Every header says what's inside it. The receiver follows the labels and never guesses.

Routers in the middle open only the outer layer, like a courier's depot. A router takes off the Ethernet header, reads the destination IP address and lowers the TTL by one. Then it wraps the packet in a new Ethernet header addressed to the next card on the next link. It never reads TCP or HTTP. That's why the MAC addresses change at every hop (one link of the journey), while the IP addresses and ports arrive untouched. It's also why each layer can change without the others noticing: HTTP doesn't know whether it crossed a cable, Wi-Fi or a mobile network.

Each layer's unit has its own name. HTTP sends a message, TCP a segment, IP a packet and Ethernet a frame, which is everything on the wire, headers included. The stepper below follows a real 140-byte frame, caught in the Try it by tcpdump, a program that records every frame that passes through a network card. It's built in the lab box, passed on by a router and unwrapped at the server.

Now we know what the request looks like as it leaves. But by the time it leaves, the clock has been running for a while. Next, we'll find out what it was waiting for.

try.title: Find the headers in a real frame
steps: In the lab box, run the capture below. tcpdump saves every frame on port 80 to a file while curl fetches the page. Port 80 carries plain HTTP, so you can read the request. Over HTTPS, encryption would scramble it.

The last command prints the frame that carries the GET in hex: each byte as two characters from 0 to 9 and a to f, 16 bytes per line. Counting from byte 0, mark where each header starts: Ethernet at byte 0, IP at byte 14 (look for 45), TCP at byte 34 (0x22) and HTTP where GET appears.
Check two fields by hand. Bytes 12 and 13 should be 0800 (IPv4 inside), and byte 23, IP's protocol field, should be 06 (TCP inside).

On a Mac, tcpdump needs sudo, which runs a command as the administrator, and Wi-Fi is usually en0. Run sudo tcpdump -i en0 -nn -e -XX -c 4 'tcp port 80' in one Terminal tab and curl -s http://example.com/ > /dev/null in another.

video.title: Envelopes inside envelopes: how one request is wrapped and read

sections.h: Three waits before the request leaves: the name, the connection and the encryption
sections.html:
Go back to the moment you press Enter, before any of those 140 bytes exist. Three things must happen first, and each one costs at least one round trip. A round trip is the time for a message to reach the other end and for an answer to come back. Inside one building full of servers, it takes well under a millisecond, a thousandth of a second. Between the east and west coasts of the US, it's about 70 ms. From the lab box to example.com's nearest server, it was about 9 ms.

First comes DNS. The kernel can't fill in an IP header without an IP address, so curl asks a resolver what example.com is. A resolver is a server whose job is to look names up, like a phone book you can call. The question and its answer cost one round trip, or more if the resolver has to ask other servers first.

Second comes TCP's handshake. Before TCP can number and resend bytes, both sides must agree where the numbering starts, and each must know that the other is there. So the client, the side that starts the conversation, sends a SYN (short for synchronize). The server answers with a SYN-ACK (synchronize, and acknowledged), and the client confirms with an ACK. The request can travel right behind that last step, so the handshake costs one round trip.

Third, for HTTPS, comes TLS (Transport Layer Security), the layer that encrypts everything so that nobody on the way can read it. The two sides agree on secret keys, and the client checks the server's certificate, a document vouched for by a company your computer trusts, which proves the server really is example.com. With TLS 1.3, the current version, that costs one more round trip, plus some time for the arithmetic.

Only then does the request leave. The first byte of the answer arrives one round trip later, plus whatever time the server spends on its own work. curl can time each step. It prints each number as seconds since it started, so each one includes all the steps before it:

dns 0.012801  connect 0.021870  tls 0.038789  first byte 0.052085  total 0.052110
Step Done at Took What happened
DNS 12.8 ms 12.8 ms a resolver turned example.com into an IP address
TCP connect 21.9 ms 9.1 ms SYN out, SYN-ACK back: one round trip
TLS 38.8 ms 16.9 ms keys and certificate: a round trip, plus the arithmetic
First byte 52.1 ms 13.3 ms the request went out and the answer started coming back

Three quarters of the total had passed before a single byte of the request left the machine. That's the trap from the café. When a page is slow, we blame the server, because it's the only part we can name. Here the server's share is at most 13.3 ms of the 52.1, and about 9 of those are the last round trip.

The fix is to pay for the setup once. Ask curl for the same page twice in one run, and the second request reuses the connection that the first one opened:

dns 0.002230  connect 0.011069  tls 0.028304  first byte 0.041567  total 0.041588
dns 0.000007  connect 0.000000  tls 0.000000  first byte 0.014657  total 0.014677

No lookup, no handshake and no TLS: 14.7 ms instead of 41.6. Opening a connection costs more than using one. Open it once, and reuse it. Programs that call one server again and again keep a few connections open between requests, in a connection pool. Then only the first request on each connection pays for DNS, TCP and TLS. Lessons 7, 9 and 10 of this track open the three waits one by one. For now, it's enough to know they're there.

So far, our request has fit in one frame. Next, we'll send something bigger, and see how TCP cuts it up and what your code sees of it.

try.title: Time your own request
steps: In the lab box, run the first two curl commands below. The first line saves a format in F, and -w tells curl to print its times in that format. For each step, subtract the number before it to get how long that step took.
Before you run the last command, predict which numbers will be zero on its second line of output. It fetches the page twice over one connection.
The same curl -w works in the Terminal app on a Mac, so you can compare your laptop with the box.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: F='dns %{time_namelookup} connect %{time_connect} tls %{time_appconnect} first byte %{time_starttransfer} total %{time_total}\n' curl -s -o /dev/null -w "$F" https://example.com/ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "$F" https://example.com/ # two URLs in one curl: the second transfer reuses the first connection curl -s -o /dev/null -o /dev/null -w "$F" https://example.com/ https://example.com/

try.expect:
From one run:

dns 0.012801  connect 0.021870  tls 0.038789  first byte 0.052085  total 0.052110
dns 0.001816  connect 0.011730  tls 0.031320  first byte 0.048113  total 0.048143
dns 0.002230  connect 0.011069  tls 0.028304  first byte 0.041567  total 0.041588
dns 0.000007  connect 0.000000  tls 0.000000  first byte 0.014657  total 0.014677

Your numbers depend on your network and on how far you are from the server, so look at the shape, not the values. DNS drops to about 2 ms on the second run, because the resolver kept the answer from the first one (it cached it). On the last line, connect and TLS are zero: the connection was already open, so only the request itself was paid for.

sections.h: Cut into packets on the wire, one stream of bytes in your code
sections.html:
Our request fit in one frame. A 1 MB answer (a million bytes, about the size of a small photo) doesn't, because every link limits how big a frame can be.

The limit has two reasons. While one frame is being sent, it holds the cable or the radio channel, and nobody else can send. And every card must keep room in its memory for the largest frame it might receive. So Ethernet settled on at most 1,500 bytes of payload per frame, where the payload is everything after the Ethernet header. That number is the link's MTU, its maximum transmission unit, and it hasn't changed on ordinary Ethernet since the 1980s.

So something must cut big data into pieces that fit, and that's TCP's job. Take 20 bytes of IP header and 20 bytes of TCP header off the 1,500, and 1,460 bytes of data fit in one segment. TCP tells the other side this number, its MSS (maximum segment size), when it opens a connection, and the capture shows mss 1460. Here both sides also switched on TCP timestamps, an option that adds 12 bytes to every TCP header. That's why our TCP header had 32 bytes, and why 1,448 bytes of data travel in each full packet. A 1 MB answer arrives as about 700 packets.

Here our parcel picture breaks. A post office never cuts a long letter into numbered strips and glues them back together at the other end. Nor does it notice a lost parcel and send a copy. TCP does both.

And your code sees none of the packets. A program sends with write(), a function that hands bytes to a socket. The program at the other end calls read() and gets bytes back. In between, TCP decides where to cut, numbers every byte, sends again what gets lost and puts the pieces back in order. So the receiver sees one long stream of bytes, with no marks where one message ends and the next begins. One write() of 4,000 bytes can come out as three read()s. One read() can return the end of one message and the start of the next. That's why every protocol built on TCP marks where its messages end. HTTP does it with a Content-Length line, which says how many bytes the body has, or by sending the body in chunks that each start with their length.

The capture of one small curl shows a whole TCP conversation: 11 packets, for a 74-byte request and a 936-byte answer. Three open the connection (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK). Then come the request, an acknowledgment of it, the answer and an acknowledgment of that. Four more close the connection: each side sends a FIN (short for finish), and each acknowledges the other's. Only two of the eleven carry any data.

One habit to take from this. When write() returns, the kernel has only copied your bytes into its own memory. It may not have sent them yet. It can't know whether they arrived, and it certainly can't tell you whether the other program acted on them. If your program sends a payment, only an answer from the other program tells you the payment arrived.

The Try it below counts those eleven packets in the capture you made earlier.

try.title: Count the packets of one curl
steps: Read the capture from the Try it in the envelopes section again with the command below. It prints one line per packet. If you've closed the box since, run that capture again first, because the file lived inside the box.

Label every line: handshake, request, answer, acknowledgment or close. The flags tell you which: [S] is a SYN, [S.] a SYN-ACK (the dot means ACK), [.] a bare ACK, [P.] a segment that carries data, and [F.] a FIN.
Find the mss value in each of the first two lines. Predict before you look: will they match?

Eleven lines (TCP options trimmed here):

... IP 172.20.0.2.57236 > 104.20.23.154.80: Flags [S], seq 3030484347, win 64240, options [mss 1460,...], length 0
... IP 104.20.23.154.80 > 172.20.0.2.57236: Flags [S.], seq 2979058730, ack 3030484348, win 65408, options [mss 65495,...], length 0
... IP 172.20.0.2.57236 > 104.20.23.154.80: Flags [.], ack 1, win 502, ..., length 0
... IP 172.20.0.2.57236 > 104.20.23.154.80: Flags [P.], seq 1:75, ack 1, win 502, ..., length 74: HTTP: GET / HTTP/1.1

Only two lines carry data (length 74 and length 936). The box's SYN says mss 1460, the Ethernet number. The SYN-ACK says mss 65495, which no Ethernet link has. On Docker Desktop, your container's TCP connection ends inside a program Docker runs to carry container traffic out, and that program opens a second connection from your Mac to the server. It's a first hint that "the other end" of a connection isn't always the machine you think.

refs.title: High Performance Browser Networking: Building blocks of TCP

opening:
Picture yourself at a café with a laptop. You type the address of a web page, press Enter, and the page appears in about 50 milliseconds, a twentieth of a second. The computer that sent it may be in another country, behind cables and machines owned by strangers.

It's easy to picture one long wire from your laptop to that computer, with your request rushing along it in one piece. The screen suggests it: you ask, the page arrives. So when a page is slow, we blame the far end. In fact, your request travels in three envelopes, one inside the other, and each machine on the way reads only the outside one. And three quarters of those 50 milliseconds pass before it leaves the laptop.

The Foundations track ended with a hint: when a request is slow or fails, look one layer down, in the network. In this lesson, we'll design a network from one cable up, take one real request apart, and time each wait before it. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at a café table, with a page that seemed to arrive in one step. It came in three envelopes, passed between machines that each read only the outside one, and it spent three quarters of its time waiting to leave.

Try it on a site you use every day. Take the first two lines of the "Time your own request" Try it, put that site's address in place of example.com, and run them in Terminal. How much of the time passes before your request leaves?

Next, we'll open the bottom row of the table, the link. Your computer knows the gateway's IP address, so how does it find the MAC address to write on the outermost envelope?

compare.title: The same request, as curl shows it and as the wire carries it

a.label: curl -v
a.title: what the application wrote
a.html:
> GET / HTTP/1.1
> Host: example.com
> User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
> Accept: */*
>

compare.note: Both show the same 74 bytes of HTTP. curl prints them as lines of text, each starting with >. On the wire, the same text starts at byte 66 (4745 5420, "GET "), after 66 bytes that curl never sees: 14 of Ethernet, 20 of IP and 32 of TCP. The kernel wrote all of those, which is why the lab reads them out of the frame, not out of curl's output.

steps.say: Take the 140-byte GET frame from the Try it. The first 14 bytes are the Ethernet header: the destination MAC, the source MAC and the EtherType. The destination comes first, so that a switch, the box that joins the cables of one link, can decide where to send the frame as soon as the first bytes arrive.
steps.code:
0x0000:  22d2 d5a2 32a3 b699 4ab0 807f 0800 4500

22 d2 d5 a2 32 a3   destination MAC 22:d2:d5:a2:32:a3 (the gateway)
b6 99 4a b0 80 7f   source MAC b6:99:4a:b0:80:7f (the lab box)
08 00               EtherType 0x0800: an IPv4 packet follows

steps.say: IP starts at byte 14. Its first byte, 45, holds two numbers, one per hex digit. The left digit, 4, is the version. The right digit, 5, is the header's length in 4-byte words, so 20 bytes. The other fields follow in a fixed order.
steps.code:
45         version 4, header length 5 x 4 = 20 bytes
00         type of service
00 7e      total length 126 = 20 IP + 32 TCP + 74 data
43 d4      identification
40 00      flags: Don't Fragment set; fragment offset 0
40         TTL 64
06         protocol 6: TCP follows
ca e1      header checksum
ac 14 00 02  source 172.20.0.2
68 14 17 9a  destination 104.20.23.154

steps.say: TCP starts at byte 14 + 20 = 34 (0x22). The ports come first. Then come two 32-bit counters: the sequence number, which numbers the bytes this side sends, and the acknowledgment number, which says how much of the other side's data has arrived. The left hex digit of byte 46 is TCP's header length in words: 8, so 32 bytes, of which 12 are options. Byte 47 holds the flags.
steps.code:
df 94        source port 57236
00 50        destination port 80
b4 a1 85 7c  sequence number 3030484348
b1 90 d4 2b  acknowledgment number 2979058731
80           header length 8 x 4 = 32 bytes
18           flags 0x18 = PSH (0x08) + ACK (0x10)
01 f6        window 502
2c 35        checksum (left for the card to finish, see Go deeper)
00 00        urgent pointer
01 01 08 0a 3c5b486f a9c964c0   options: NOP, NOP, timestamps

steps.say: The application's data starts at 14 + 20 + 32 = 66, which is 0x42. That's where 47 45 54 20 spells GET and a space. From there to the end, 74 bytes, is exactly what curl wrote. The lab asks you to write this walk as code.

lab.title: Peel a captured frame layer by layer
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All 12 fail with NotImplementedError, Kotlin's way of saying a function's body is still a TODO. Then open src/test/resources/sfz/net/l01/http-get.txt: it's the frame from the Try it, exactly as tcpdump printed it, and the tests read it from there.
Read Layers.kt. Its classes are finished, one per layer, and each field's comment says which bytes it comes from.

In Decapsulate.kt, write parseEthernet, then parseIpv4, then parseTcp. Wrap the bytes in a ByteBuffer, a Java class that reads two or four bytes at a time as one number. Widen every number before you store it: Kotlin's Byte, Short and Int can be negative, but no field on the wire ever is.
Write ipv4Checksum, and check it against cae1, the value the kernel wrote into the captured header.
Write decapsulate. It checks each layer's "what's inside" field (the EtherType, then the protocol) before it hands the payload to the next parser. Run the tests until all 12 pass.
hints: ByteBuffer.wrap(bytes).getShort(12).toInt() and 0xffff reads bytes 12 and 13 as one number that is never negative. Without the and 0xffff, port 57236 comes out negative, because a Short only goes up to 32,767.
The sequence numbers are bigger than an Int can hold (above 2^31). Read them with getInt(4).toLong() and 0xffffffffL.
IP's header length is bytes[0].toInt() and 0x0f, counted in 4-byte words. TCP's is the left hex digit of its byte 12: (bytes[12].toInt() and 0xff) shr 4, also in words.
Cut the IP payload with copyOfRange(headerLength, totalLength), not up to size. One test adds padding to the frame: zero bytes that Ethernet puts after a short packet, which aren't part of it.

For the checksum, add each 16-bit word (two bytes) into a Long, skipping bytes 10 and 11, the checksum itself. Fold with while (sum shr 16 != 0L) sum = (sum and 0xffff) + (sum shr 16) and return sum.inv().toInt() and 0xffff.

drill.title: Draw the frame from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking back, write the layers of the GET frame from the outside in. For each one, give its header size in this capture, the field that says what's inside it, and the pair of addresses it carries. Then add up the sizes and check them against the answer.

answer.html:
Ethernet  14 bytes   EtherType 0x0800 = IPv4   MACs   b6:99:4a:b0:80:7f > 22:d2:d5:a2:32:a3 (box > gateway)
IPv4      20 bytes   protocol 6 = TCP          IPs    172.20.0.2 > 104.20.23.154
TCP       32 bytes   port 80 = the web server  ports  57236 > 80
HTTP      74 bytes                             name   Host: example.com
total    140 bytes on the wire, plus a 4-byte checksum the card adds at the end, which tcpdump never shows

recap: Four layers, four kinds of address: a name for people, a port for the program, an IP address for the computer, and a MAC address for the next card on this link. DNS turns the name into an IP address.
Each layer adds a header on the way down and removes it on the way up. The EtherType, the IP protocol number and the port say what's inside, so the receiver never guesses.
Every router writes new MAC addresses for the next link. The IP addresses and ports travel unchanged from end to end, unless a box on the way rewrites them (lesson 3 of this track meets one).
Before a request is even sent, it waits for DNS, TCP's handshake and TLS, each at least one round trip. curl -w times each step, and a reused connection skips all three.

Ethernet's MTU is 1,500 bytes, so TCP cuts what you send into segments of at most 1,460 bytes of data. Your code sees one stream of bytes, never packets, and a finished write() only means the kernel has your bytes.

The limit: this picture is one request on a quiet network. It shows where each address lives, not how a computer learns the next card's MAC, how routers choose a path, or what TCP does when packets go missing. Each later lesson opens one row of the table.

explain.prompt: A friend who is new to networks looks at the frame that carried your request. They ask why its destination MAC belongs to the router at the edge of your network, the gateway, and not to the web server. Explain it in your own words, and say where the server's address is.
explain.answer: A MAC address only works on one link: it tells the cards that can hear each other which one should take the frame. The web server is many links away, so my computer can't address its card. The kernel sees that the server's IP address isn't on my own link, so it hands the frame to the default gateway, by putting the gateway's MAC on the outside. The server's address is in the IP header, one envelope further in, and it stays there the whole way. Every router on the path takes the Ethernet header off, reads the IP address to choose the next hop, and wraps the packet in a new Ethernet header for the next link.

deeper.html:
Why tcpdump calls your TCP checksum wrong. Run tcpdump -vv -r /tmp/get.pcap, and every packet the box sent shows something like cksum 0x2c35 (incorrect -> 0x85e6). Nothing is broken. Linux leaves the TCP checksum for the network card to finish, which is called checksum offload, and tcpdump copies the packet before that happens. In the lab box, ethtool -k eth0 | grep checksum shows tx-checksumming: on. The IP header's checksum is different: the kernel works it out itself, which is why the lab can check it against the capture.

Segments bigger than the MTU. During a big download, you may see TCP segments of 20,000 bytes or more in tcpdump. That's segmentation offload: the kernel hands the card (or the virtual card in a container) one large segment, and it's cut into MTU-sized frames below the point where tcpdump watches. The wire never carries more than 1,500 bytes of payload per frame. ethtool -k eth0 | grep segmentation shows it switched on in the lab box.

Where the OSI model went. OSI was designed from the late 1970s as a complete set of protocols, and it lost to TCP/IP. Its numbering stuck because textbooks taught it everywhere. Its layers 5 and 6, session and presentation, have no protocol of their own in the internet's stack: TLS is sometimes called layer 6, but it runs inside the application. QUIC, the newer protocol under HTTP/3, does the work of TCP and TLS in one protocol that runs on top of UDP, and it fits no layer diagram. Use the numbers as vocabulary and no further.

The checksum at the end of every frame. Each Ethernet frame ends with a 4-byte checksum, a CRC-32 called the frame check sequence. The receiving card works it out again, drops frames that don't match, and strips it off before the kernel sees the frame, so captures almost never show it. A climbing RX errors count in ip -s link show eth0 is how a bad cable or a noisy Wi-Fi link shows up.
